Joseph Myers said:

There should be lots of ways for AI to accelerate stating things other than building a sloplib. For example, AI could probably help with many of the more mechanical parts of PR review for mathlib (that aren't mechanical enough to turn into linters) and so reduce the amount of time maintainers need to spend on those when doing reviews for mathlib. People have written extremely detailed instructions to AIs on Linux kernel patch review, why shouldn't we have similarly detailed instructions on reviewing mathlib changes and a service that does such reviews on PRs (automatically, or when requested)?

Oh, and we have this too! See https://github.com/kim-em/botbaki. You can actually use it today on mathlib, try @botbaki review on a PR to request a review, and then @botbaki feedback ... (or just emojis) to tell it whether the review was any good. There's a backend process to incorporate the feedback into a revised review prompt.

The prompting currently is very simplistic, but I think it would be a great project to improve it.

Are you saying it's currently active on Mathlib? I've just tried to trigger it on #34559 out of curiosity, but it doesn't look like anything is happening.
Now that botbaki has reviewed #34559, I see it's suggesting omega (to be avoided nowadays) and changing a terminal simp (for a subgoal) to simp only (also typically discouraged).

I restarted the listener and it has now responded.

Joseph Myers said:

Now that botbaki has reviewed #34559, I see it's suggesting omega (to be avoided nowadays) and changing a terminal simp (for a subgoal) to simp only (also typically discouraged).

@Joseph Myers, maybe you would like to reply to those comments with @botbaki feedback ..., and I will then see what prompting updates we get.

Or just giving +1 / -1 emoji reactions to its comments should work as well.

The result is quite nice: it caught two real mistakes (repeated scope opening, misnamed lemma) and gave two bad suggestions (unhappy with a grind [StrictMonoOn] proof, wanted to turn a terminal simp into a simp only). Will it improve if we train it on a few PRs and give feedback? If so, I think it's definitely worth investigating.

@Kim Morrison , what do you think about incorporating https://github.com/Vilin97/mathlib-conventions into botbaki? I am happy to improve my methodology but the core idea is to mine all the suggestions that mathlib maintainers ever made and distill them into a single list of rules.
I assume that you hand-wrote botbaki's guidelines, which might miss some rules. I assembled some rules that botbaki misses here. For example, the guideline "Put declarations in their canonical home" has been repeated by maintainers 730 times but is missing from botbaki's review prompt.

I made a PR to botbaki adding the 12 most frequent guidelines that are missing from botbaki's prompt: https://github.com/kim-em/botbaki/pull/1
I tried botbaki to review my PR. It gave two suggestions, both bad. It thinks grind is still experimental and that the module tactic does not exist.
@Vasily Ilin, I have commented on your PR.
Is this still running? If so, is there a way to run it on repositories other than Mathlib? I'd like to try this out on some CGT PRs where I can't find human reviewers :frown:

No, sorry.

You could of course write a roadmap for TauCeti for the material, then send the PRs to TauCeti, where they will be reviewed by something much better than botbaki ever was, and then take your material back to your human-curated library afterwards!
Couldn't one just fork TauCetiReview and adapt it to become a reviewer bot for any project (as botbaki)? Or is it inherently tied to the roadmap system somehow?

Possibly! There is one rubric that explicitly refers to checking that it fits against a nominated roadmap, so you could drop that.

But I do not promise TauCetiReview will not in future rely on weird non-standard bits of Tau Ceti infrastructure as the project grows!

I did make a fork now on Tau Ceti Review to run on any project:
https://github.com/felixpernegger/lean-review

Obviously it's completely vibe coded (with Opus 5.5) and not tested very thoroughly (in particular I only tested with Claude Code), but it appears to be working. :)

Maybe I will update it once in a while, but probably not...
